content.text: Initial search terms were constructed around "intercept adjustment" and "in sample error". These terms are combined to refine the search. The goal is to identify relevant academic papers published through late 2026.

The current calculation appears limited to in-sample error correction, without demonstrating generalizability to unseen data. This raises concerns about its broader applicability and novelty. It's crucial to find research that addresses whether the mean residual correction offers improvements beyond the specific dataset provided, which would align with the overall project objective.

Efron's work on biased error rates and covariance penalties highlight the inherent issues with in-sample evaluation and the optimism it introduces. Stone's contribution further supports that held-out validation is critical to avoid biased assessment. Cox's work on intercept adjustment offers a basis for calibration but with limitations regarding generalizability.

These papers emphasize the critical distinction between in-sample and out-of-sample performance, particularly concerning the optimism of in-sample validation. The studies highlight that intercept-only adjustments can address mean bias in a given sample, but don't guarantee improved generalizability to unseen data, aligning with the need for validation hierarchies and recalibration. Smaller sample sizes further exacerbate the underestimation of out-of-sample error, suggesting the need to address the problem of limited data samples.

The calibration hierarchy from Boer et al. (2016) underscores that intercept adjustment only addresses mean error within the existing data and not generalizability. Vergouwe et al. (2017) formalizes tests to select appropriate model updating methods, showing the risks of overfitting with intercept-only adjustments. Harrell et al. (1996) explains why derivation-cohort performance is overly optimistic and cannot establish out-of-sample validity.

The analysis indicates that evaluating goodness-of-fit and calibration exclusively on the training data poses a risk. Quantifying this bias, particularly in the context of intercept adjustments, requires explicit correction due to degrees of freedom used during parameter estimation. Maximizing likelihood or minimizing error on the observed data leads to an overly optimistic evaluation biased by the dimension of adjusted parameters, mathematically demonstrating the necessity of penalizing in-sample error to infer out-of-sample error.
